newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus rise fans friction fears before G7.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus rise fans friction fears before G7.

text.p: A big jump in Japan's external surplus fanned trade friction fears on Wednesday as Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto prepares for a summit meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations next week.

The surplus in the current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen ($9.8 billion) in April from a year ago as higher taxes dampened imports and the strong U.S. economy sucked in Japanese goods, government data showed.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 90.9 percent from a year earlier to 1.02 trillion yen ($9.1 billion).

The surge in the surplus had been widely anticipated and intially caused only a ripple on financial markets. But the United States quickly sounded a warning about the growing trade gap, stoking up trade friction jitters and sending the dollar tumbling to almost seven-month lows below 111 yen.

U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said in a speech to be delivered to a trade group in Denver that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth, and should foster demand-led recovery at home.

Earlier this week, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky expressed concern about what she called "disturbing" trends in Japan's trade balance and repeated that Washington did not want a big rise in Japan's surplus.

But some economists said the outlook was for a rising surplus. "Japan's surplus is on a very rapid widening trend. We had a widening surplus in the last seven months with the United States. What is taking place here, is suddenly a big explosion in the surplus vis-a-vis Europe, and even with Asia," Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
"A very straight-forward way of looking at the issue is that Japan wants help from external demand to help its economic recovery," said Mamoru Yamaguchi, an economist at Nikko Research Center.

Japanese officials have said that the nation's economic recovery may suffer a temporary setback from a rise in the consumption tax that took effect on April 1. But they say the recovery is still on track, centering on domestic demand.

"Japan's top business leaders have said that a dollar rate of 110 to 120 yen was desirable. I think the government also believes that this range is where Japan can receive merits of a weak yen without being criticised by the United States," Yamaguchi said.
He expects repeated warnings about Japan's external surplus from top U.S. officials ahead of an expected slowdown in the U.S. economy later this year. A weaker dollar helps American exports.

G7 officials in Washington said on Monday that U.S. President Bill Clinton is not expected to be as forceful on the subject as he was when he met Hashimoto in April, if the issue comes up in a bilateral meeting during the G7 summit in Denver from June 20-22.
Since April, the dollar has tumbled against the yen and Japan's economy has looked stronger than expected -- two developments that will cap the rise in Japan's surplus.
A Finance Ministry official told reporters that the surplus was unlikely to rise significantly in the medium to longer term.

Andrew Shipley, economist at Schroders Japan Ltd, also saw the rise as a short-term phenomenon. "We see the increase in the surplus as a temporary development, certainly to end by the first half of the current fiscal year," he said.
